The next island was low and wooded, with a thread of smoke rising from the middle of the forest.
Nobody wanted to go and look, and you can't blame them.
The last two times they'd gone to look, giants had eaten them.
So they drew lots, and half the crew went, led by a man named Eurylochus.
Deep in the forest they found a house of polished stone.
Lions and wolves prowled around it, but they didn't attack. They came up wagging their tails like dogs.
Inside, a woman was singing at a loom.
Her name was Circe. She invited them in and gave them cheese and honey and wine.
Only Eurylochus stayed outside, because something about it felt wrong to him.
Once they'd drunk it, Circe touched each of them with a wand and they turned into pigs, with the heads and the bristles and the grunting.
Their minds stayed human, which is the cruel part.
She drove them into a sty and threw them acorns.
Eurylochus ran all the way back to the ship. Odysseus picked up his sword and went alone.
On the path a young man stopped him. It was Hermes, messenger of the gods, sent to help.
He gave Odysseus a little plant with a black root and a white flower, called moly.
Eat this, he said, and her drug won't touch you.
And when she raises that wand, draw your sword as if you're going to kill her.
Circe touched him with the wand and said: now go and lie down with your friends in the sty.
He drew his sword, and Circe dropped to her knees, because she understood who he was.
You must be Odysseus, she said. Hermes always told me you'd come.
She turned his men back, younger and taller than before, and then she asked them all to stay.
In the end it was his own men who had to remind him. Odysseus, they said, remember home.
When he asked Circe to let him go, she said he was free to leave, but he couldn't go home yet.
First he had to go somewhere no living man had ever been: the house of the dead.
They sailed to the end of the world, where the sun never shines, to the edge of the river Ocean.
Odysseus dug a pit in the ground with his sword and poured offerings into it: milk and honey, then wine, then water, then barley.
Then he cut the throats of a ram and a black ewe and let their blood run into the pit.
And the dead came up out of the dark in their thousands.
There were brides and young men, old men who'd suffered a lot, soldiers still in their bloody armour,
all of them making a terrible noise and pushing toward the blood.
The dead are empty in Homer. Only blood lets them remember who they were, and speak.
Odysseus held them back with his sword, because he was waiting for one particular ghost.
The first to reach him was Elpenor, the youngest of his crew.
On their last night at Circe's he'd gone to sleep drunk on the roof,
and in the morning he forgot where he was, stepped off the edge, and broke his neck.
They'd sailed without even noticing he was gone. He begged Odysseus to go back and bury him.
Then came someone Odysseus didn't expect at all. His mother.
She'd been alive when he left for Troy.
He kept her back with the sword too.
He let her stand there and wouldn't let her drink, because the one he'd come for hadn't arrived yet.
I find that one of the hardest moments in the whole poem.
At last Tiresias came, the blind prophet, carrying a golden staff.
He drank the blood, and he told Odysseus the truth.
Poseidon will never forgive you for his son, he said.
But you can still get home, you and your men, if you manage one thing.
On the island of the Sun you'll find the Sun god's cattle.
Leave them alone, and you'll all get home.
Touch them, and your ship will be destroyed and your men will die,
and you'll come home late, alone, on a stranger's ship,
and find men in your house eating your bread and courting your wife.
Only then did he let his mother drink.
She knew him straight away. She told him she hadn't died of illness or old age.
She'd died of missing him, waiting for him to come home.
Three times he reached out to hold her, and three times she slipped through his arms like a shadow, or a dream.
Agamemnon, the king who'd led the whole war, murdered in his own house by his own wife on the day he came home.
And then Achilles, the greatest of all the Greeks.
Odysseus tried to comfort him. Nobody was ever as lucky as you, he said.
When you were alive we honoured you like a god, and down here you're a king among the dead.
Achilles told him not to try to make death sound good.
He said he'd rather be the poorest hired hand on earth, working a field for a man with nothing, than be king over all of the dead.
Odysseus climbed back up to the light with that answer in his ears.
